Lessons.Title: Relative Frequency Tables
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: calculate joint, row-conditional and column-conditional relative frequencies in a two-way table, identify each denominator and translate percentages into context. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U03:L02, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/3/2/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0); Addressing HSS-ID.B.5. The source distinguishes three valid percentage questions that have different reference populations.

Reuse the independent fictional club dataset only as a labelled mathematical bridge: A Sports12/Arts8 total20; B Sports9/Arts11 total20; Sports column21; Arts column19; overall40. Joint frequency for Group A and Sports is 12/40=30%. Within A, Sports frequency 12/20=60%; among all Sports respondents, the proportion in A is 12/21≈57.14%. These are different claims.

Student task: construct three separately titled relative-frequency tables using the overall sample, row and column denominators, calculate complements, and explain why 30%, 60% and 57.14% can all describe the same interior cell without disagreement. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for denominator selection, correct row/column calculations, labelled percentages and justified comparison and critique.

V12 source-specific relative frequency representations: use the independent 40-response club table Group A [Sports12, Arts8] and Group B [Sports9, Arts11]. The JOINT table by grand total40 is A Sports30%, A Arts20%, B Sports22.5%, B Arts27.5%, whose cells sum100%. The ROW-CONDITIONAL tables are A [60%,40%] and B [45%,55%]; the COLUMN-CONDITIONAL tables are Sports [A12/21≈57.14%, B9/21≈42.86%], Arts [A8/19≈42.11%, B11/19≈57.89%]. Teacher and student sources: https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/3/2/preparation.html and https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/3/2/index.html.

V12 student task: draw three original segmented-bar representations from the separate joint, row and column percentages; label the reference populations and horizontal/vertical denominators. Explain why the percentages for A Sports differ (30%,60%,57.14%) without contradicting each other. The published unit includes segmented bars and a Notice and Wonder, so a frequency table alone does not complete its visual activity.

Draft teacher rubric0–2 each for joint-cell/whole sums, row/column denominators and totals, actual segmented bar graphs with labels, and contextual conditional probability reasoning. Visual learner artifact and teacher grading remain unverified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Joint relative frequency
KeyConcepts.Definition: An interior count divided by grand total.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Name both categories and the overall reference population.

KeyConcepts.Title: Row conditional frequency
KeyConcepts.Definition: A cell divided by its row total.

KeyConcepts.Title: Column conditional frequency
KeyConcepts.Definition: A cell divided by its column total.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find joint frequency
WorkedExamples.Question: What fraction of all40 are in A and Sports?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the first-party data, compute with the correct denominator, and interpret with sample limitations.
Steps: Interpret as 30% of whole hypothetical sample.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare row percentages
WorkedExamples.Question: What percent of A and B choose Sports?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the first-party data, compute with the correct denominator, and interpret with sample limitations.
Steps: A has12 Sports out of20, giving12/20=60%.
B has9 Sports out of20, giving9/20=45%.
The percentages refer to different groups but same category.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both denominators are their own row totals20.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute conditional by column
WorkedExamples.Question: Of21 Sports respondents, what fraction belong to A?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the first-party data, compute with the correct denominator, and interpret with sample limitations.
Steps: Twelve of these belong to A.
Do not divide by A total20; that answers a different question.
WorkedExamples.Answer: About57.14% of Sports respondents are in A.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using overall denominator for a conditional percentage
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That answers a joint rather than conditional question.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming percentage-point difference as relative percent increase
CommonMistakes.Correction: Name the measure correctly and show denominators.

SummaryPoints: Joint, row and column frequencies use distinct denominators.
The same cell can yield 30%,60% or57.14%, depending on reference group.
Row-based values can be compared to inspect possible association.
Human explanation of the relevant population is part of assessment.
